content.text: Students build on earlier lessons about myth adaptation, threshold crossing, and transformation to study the emotional aftermath of Percy’s arrival in the mythic world.
Myths and myth-inspired stories help people explore danger, grief, identity, and belonging, and each version of a story can shape those ideas differently.
This lesson prepares students for Lesson 13, when they will study the culture and rules of Camp Half-Blood more closely.
Students will need to trace how a theme develops across part of a narrative and explain how different versions shape meaning.

The Minotaur on Page and Screen

You will use a T-chart to help us compare the same scene in the book and the movie. First, return to the part of the novel where Percy faces the Minotaur in the storm. Then you will watch the matching film scene twice. The first time, notice the overall feeling. The second time, record what you see and hear in your T-chart so you can compare how each medium creates mood.
Label the T-chart columns as indicated:
Under each column, you should note:
In the section where Percy first faces the Minotaur, which description in the novel most strongly creates a mood for the reader? What is that mood?
Is that similar to or different from how the film made you feel? What moves from the film helped you feel that way?
What do you hear in the film that helps create the tone?
to explain one important difference between how the novel and film create fear.
Which statement best explains how the film version of the Minotaur encounter changes the mood?
The film and novel create exactly the same mood because both include the same monster.
The film makes the scene less intense because viewers can see the full setting more clearly.

While the film uses lighting, sound, and actor expressions to make the danger feel immediate, the novel builds fear through Percy’s thoughts and descriptions, which creates a different kind of terrifying mood.
The scene in the novel is more frightening because it takes longer to read than the clip takes to watch.

Today, you looked at some of the ways the creators of stories can shape mood: through word choice in the novel and through visual and sound choices in the film. Use one detail from Chapter 5 and one detail from the film clip to explain how Percy’s world feels different across the two versions.
How do the novel and film create different emotional responses to Percy’s encounter with the mythic world? Cite at least two specific details, including one from the text and one from the film.
Have students take out their Lesson 11 notes or paragraphs and keep Chapter 5 open. Invite partners to begin focusing on Percy’s emotional world, not just surface-level plot events.
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the question.
At the start of Chapter 5, what emotions might Percy be carrying with him into camp, and why? Cite evidence from Chapter 5 to support your ideas.

Percy is probably carrying grief, confusion, and fear. He has just lost his mother, fought the Minotaur, and woke up in a place he does not understand, so even a safe place would still feel strange to him.
Now that we’ve named how Percy feels, we’ll use context clues and precise emotional language to explain how Riordan creates the mood in this part of the story.
Students will activate thinking about Percy’s emotional state after the Minotaur attack and connect Lesson 11’s focus on transformation to today’s study of grief, identity, and belonging.

Learning in Action: The Minotaur on Page and Screen (RL.6.7, SL.6.2)

In this part of the lesson, students compare how the Minotaur scene is presented in the novel and in the film adaptation. They’ll learn key vocabulary for analyzing different storytelling mediums and practice noticing how visual and aural choices shape mood. This work helps them understand that a film is an interpretation, not a copy, and that directors use specific tools to influence how viewers experience a scene.
Before viewing, introduce students to key terms for comparing a novel and its film adaptation.
the form a story takes, such as a book or a movie
something the viewer can hear, including dialogue, music, and sound effects
what the director gives extra attention to
a creator’s way of understanding and presenting a story
A film adaptation does not only repeat a story. The creator of the adaptation makes careful choices about what viewers will see, hear, and feel.

Have students reread the section of text where Percy first sees and faces the Minotaur. Then show the matching film segment in short parts, replaying at least once so students can notice what they see and hear.

We will use a T-chart to help us compare the same scene in the book and the movie. First, return to the part of the novel where Percy faces the Minotaur in the storm. Then we will watch the matching film scene twice. The first time, notice the overall feeling. The second time, record what you see and hear in your T-chart so you can compare how each medium creates mood.
Label the T-chart columns as indicated:
Under each column, you should note:

When I compare a scene in a book to the same scene in a movie, I do not start by asking which one I like better. I start by asking what each medium makes me notice and think about. In the novel, Riordan helps the reader understand Percy’s fear through storm details, monster descriptions, and Percy’s thoughts. In the film, the director can use dark lighting, loud sounds, and actor expressions to make the danger feel immediate. If I notice a shadowy setting, heavy footsteps, and Percy’s panicked face, I can explain that those choices create a mood for me as a viewer. Then I compare those details to the novel and decide whether the fear feels more internal, more visual, or both.
In the section where Percy first faces the Minotaur, which description in the novel most strongly creates a mood for the reader? What is that mood?

One strong description is when Percy realizes the creature is not a normal bull but a monster charging through the storm. That detail creates a terrifying mood because the danger feels huge and unnatural right away.
Is that similar to or different from how the film made you feel? What moves from the film helped you feel that way?

I felt the same way while watching the film. The dark lighting, fast movement, and the actor’s frightened expression make the scene feel more immediate. Those visual details make it seem like the danger is happening right in front of the viewer.
What do you hear in the film that helps create the tone?
The heavy footsteps, loud music, and monster sounds help create the tone. The sound keeps building pressure, so the scene feels more threatening.
to explain one important difference between how the novel and film create fear.
Although the film uses lighting, sound, and actor expressions to create instant terror, the novel builds fear through Percy’s thoughts and descriptions, which makes the scene feel more personal.
Which statement best explains how the film version of the Minotaur encounter changes the mood?
The film and novel create exactly the same mood because both include the same monster.
Incorrect: This reflects the misconception that shared plot automatically creates the same emotional effect, even when the medium changes how the audience experiences the scene.
The film makes the scene less intense because viewers can see the full setting more clearly.
Incorrect: A student might focus on visibility alone and miss how darkness, pacing, sound, and acting create fear rather than reduce it.

While the film uses lighting, sound, and actor expressions to make the danger feel immediate, the novel builds fear through Percy’s thoughts and descriptions, which creates a different kind of terrifying mood.
This answer accurately explains how the two mediums use different tools to create fear.
The scene in the novel is more frightening because it takes longer to read than the clip takes to watch.
Incorrect: This answer confuses length with craft and ignores the specific choices authors and directors make to shape mood.
Support students in naming specific sensory details from a novel and a film and using comparative language to explain how each medium creates a terrifying mood.
Sensory language for visual and aural details
Explanation with because, although, whereas, and while
Have partners orally rehearse one sentence using the frame “Although the film ___, the novel ___ because ___.”
Prompt students to separate what they see from what they hear before they explain the mood.
If students give a reaction like “It is scarier,” prompt them to name the exact media choice that created that effect.
Name the moves that create the mood: “You said, ‘The movie makes it way more intense’—we can say, ‘The film increases the intensity through visual emphasis and sound.’”
Connect to author’s craft: “That idea connects to medium because a film can create fear with sound and images right away, while a novel relies on description and thoughts.”
The visual detail ___ creates a terrifying mood because ___.
The aural detail ___ adds fear by ___.
Although the film ___, the novel ___, which changes the mood by ___.
Invite students to name fear-related sensory words in a shared home language first, then choose the closest English term for their chart.
Encourage students to use gestures or quick facial expressions to show mood before turning that observation into academic language.
If students retell the attack without identifying a media choice → Prompt: “What exactly did you see or hear that created that feeling?”
If students confuse Percy’s thoughts in the novel with film dialogue → Prompt: “Is that detail something the reader learns from narration or something the viewer hears aloud?”
Students name a specific visual or aural detail and explain how it contributes to a terrifying mood.
Students use a contrast structure such as although, whereas, or while to compare the novel and film clearly.
Struggling with: Sorting what counts as a media choice
Give students a short checklist with lighting, music, sound effects, monster appearance, actor expression, and Percy’s thoughts.
Struggling with: Comparing the two mediums clearly
Provide the frame “Although the film ___, the novel ___ because ___” and require one specific detail in each blank.
Allow students to rehearse their answer aloud with a partner first or use speech-to-text to capture their sentence.
Ask students to explain which medium makes Percy feel more vulnerable and why. Invite students to analyze whether making the Minotaur more visually dramatic always strengthens the scene.
The Minotaur on Page and Screen (RL.6.7, SL.6.2)
Students will use a media analysis T-chart to compare how the novel and the 2010 film version create a specific mood during Percy’s encounter with the Minotaur.

Today, we looked at some of the ways the creators of stories can shape mood: through word choice in the novel and through visual and sound choices in the film. Use one detail from Chapter 5 and one detail from the film clip to explain how Percy’s world feels different across the two versions.
How do the novel and film create different emotional responses to Percy’s encounter with the mythic world? Cite at least two specific details, including one from the text and one from the film.

In Chapter 5, the novel creates an unsettled mood because Percy wakes up carrying grief and confusion, and details like the dream and the Minotaur horn keep the danger emotionally close to him. In the film, the monsters feel more immediate and terrifying because the visual effects, movement, and sound make them look openly threatening right away. Although both versions show Percy entering a mythic world, the novel emphasizes his disorientation while the film emphasizes shock and action.
Students will synthesize how word choice and media choice shape emotional response and theme development.

standards.description: Recognize variations from standard English in their own and others’ writing and speaking, and identify and use strategies to improve expression in conventional language.
Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word’s position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

Compare and contrast the experience of reading a story, drama, or poem to listening to or viewing an audio, video, or live version of the text, including contrasting what they “see” and “hear” when reading the text to what they perceive when they listen or watch.
Interpret information presented in diverse media and formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) and explain how it contributes to a topic, text, or issue under study.
Vary sentence patterns for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.

Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with light support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with substantial support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with moderate support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language resources to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the specific language used to present ideas and claims that are well supported and distinguishing them from those that are not), with light support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use language to support ideas and arguments with detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the precise vocabulary used to present evidence, or the phrasing used to signal a shift in meaning), with substantial support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., showing the clarity of the phrasing used to present an argument), with moderate support.

Use various verb types (e.g., doing, saying being/having, thinking/feeling, reporting), tenses (e.g., present, past, future, simple, progressive, perfect) appropriate to the task, text type, and discipline (e.g., the present perfect to describe previously made claims or conclusions) on a variety of topics.

Use a variety of verb types (e.g., doing, saying, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling), tenses (e.g., present, past, future, simple, progressive) appropriate to the text type and discipline (e.g., simple past and past progressive for recounting an experience) on familiar topics.

Use various verb types (e.g., doing, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling, reporting), tenses (e.g., present, past, future, simple, progressive, perfect) appropriate to the task, text type, and discipline (e.g., simple present for literary analysis) on an increasing variety of topics.
